title: Rotational kinetic energy
examples: How is rotational kinetic energy different from linear kinetic energy?
What is the relationship between torque and the work done?
Can you give an example of rotational kinetic energy in daily life?

explain.say: Today we explore rotational kinetic energy. This energy is stored in objects that spin. The formula for this energy is one half I omega squared.
The moment of inertia, I, measures how mass is distributed. A more spread out mass means a larger moment of inertia. For example, a hoop has a larger I than a solid disk.
Angular velocity, omega, is the rate of change in angle. It is measured in radians per second. Think of how fast something is spinning around its axis.
Next we look at work done by torque. Torque is the twisting force that causes rotation. Work done is calculated by the product of torque and the angle.
Consider a wrench turning a bolt. The force applied creates a torque. Applying this torque over an angle does work on the bolt.
In daily life, think about a merry-go-round. Pushing it makes it spin, giving it rotational kinetic energy. The harder you push, the more energy it has.

faq.q: Does rotational kinetic energy only apply to spinning objects?
faq.a: No, it is a form of energy for any object that rotates or spins around an axis. This concept extends to things that are not obvious spinning objects.
asks: Does it only happen when it's spinning fast?

faq.q: What is the difference between torque and force?
faq.a: Force is a push or a pull on an object. Torque is the twisting effect created by that force acting at a distance from an axis.
asks: Is torque just a bigger force?

faq.q: If I increase the moment of inertia, what happens to the energy?
faq.a: If you increase the moment of inertia while keeping other factors the same, the rotational kinetic energy will increase. More mass spread out means more energy stored.
asks: Does bigger I mean more energy?
What affects the moment of inertia?

faq.q: Is work done by torque the same as work done by force?
faq.a: They are related but not identical. Work done by force is force times distance, but work done by torque involves the angle of rotation.
asks: What is the difference between work and torque?

faq.q: What units are used for these calculations?
faq.a: Rotational kinetic energy is measured in joules, just like other forms of energy. Torque is measured in newton meters.
asks: What are the units for I?
Do I use radians or degrees for omega?

facts: Rotational kinetic energy is given by one half I omega squared.
Moment of inertia depends on both mass and the mass's distance from the axis.
Work done by torque is calculated as torque multiplied by the angular displacement.
Angular velocity, omega, must be in radians per second for calculations.

quiz.say: A spinning top has a moment of inertia of 5 kilograms meter squared and an angular velocity of 10 radians per second. What is its rotational kinetic energy?
quiz.why: You correctly used the formula one half I omega squared to find the energy.

wrong.0: You might have incorrectly used the linear kinetic energy formula.
wrong.2: You might have forgotten to square the angular velocity.
wrong.3: You may have multiplied I by omega squared instead of using one half.

quiz.say: A constant torque causes a wheel to rotate through an angle of three radians. If the torque is 15 newton meters, what is the work done?
quiz.why: The work done is the product of the constant torque and the total angle rotated.

wrong.0: You might have only used the angle value in the calculation.
wrong.1: You incorrectly added the units instead of multiplying them.
wrong.3: You might have forgotten to multiply by the angle of rotation.

quiz.say: If you double the angular velocity, how does the rotational kinetic energy change?

options.show: It increases by a factor of four
options.say: It increases by a factor of four

options.show: It increases by a factor of two
options.say: It increases by a factor of two

quiz.why: Since omega is squared in the formula, doubling it results in a factor of four increase.

wrong.0: This suggests that angular velocity has no effect on the energy stored.
wrong.2: This assumes the relationship is linear, ignoring the squared term.
wrong.3: This is a common mistake when dealing with squared variables.
